records.name: Anemic Transaction Script
records.definition: Implementing business logic as procedural scripts over data-only objects, with no rich domain model.

records.name: Implicit Integration
records.definition: Integrating contexts through undocumented, assumed connections instead of explicit, mapped relationships.

records.name: Shared Global Model
records.definition: Forcing one global model across the whole system, so unrelated parts are coupled through it.

records.name: Business Rule Encapsulation
records.definition: The ability to keep business rules inside the domain objects they govern.

records.name: Cross-Entity Domain Logic
records.definition: The ability to place logic that spans several entities in a dedicated domain service.

records.name: Domain Alignment
records.definition: The ability to keep the software model closely aligned with the business domain it serves.

records.name: Identity-Based Equality

distinctFrom.reason: Identity-based equality compares two objects by identity, while lifecycle tracking follows one object through its changes.

records.definition: The ability to treat two objects as the same when they share an identity, regardless of their attributes.

records.name: Legacy/System Integration
records.definition: The ability to integrate a legacy or external system without letting its model corrupt the domain.

records.name: Lifecycle Tracking
records.definition: The ability to track an entity as the same thing through changes over its lifetime.

records.name: Root-Guarded Invariants
records.definition: The ability to enforce an aggregate's invariants by routing all changes through its root.

records.name: Self-Validating Values

distinctFrom.reason: Self-validating values guarantee validity at construction, while side-effect-free equality compares values by content.

records.definition: The ability for a value object to guarantee its own validity at construction.

records.name: Side-Effect-Free Equality
records.definition: The ability to compare value objects by their contents with no side effects.

records.name: Transactional Consistency Boundary

distinctFrom.reason: The consistency boundary is the unit within which invariants hold atomically, while root-guarded invariants are enforced by routing every change through the root.

records.definition: The ability to treat an aggregate as the unit within which invariants hold atomically.

records.name: Explicit Boundary
records.definition: The requirement that a clear boundary separate the domain from external systems it integrates with.

records.name: Relationship Semantics
records.definition: The requirement that each relationship between bounded contexts carry a defined meaning.

records.name: Stable Identity
records.definition: The requirement that an entity keep one stable identifier throughout its lifetime.

records.name: Value Equality
records.definition: The requirement that two value objects be treated as equal when all their attributes match.

records.name: Translation Model
records.definition: A mapping between an external system's concepts and the domain's own, keeping the two vocabularies separate.

records.name: Aggregate Size
records.definition: The degree to which enlarging an aggregate to enforce invariants increases contention and load on it.

records.name: Cross-Context Reuse
records.definition: The degree to which isolating each context's model limits reusing models across contexts.

records.name: Documentation Overhead
records.definition: The degree of ongoing effort to document and maintain the map of relationships between contexts.

records.name: Domain Purity
records.definition: The degree to which the domain model stays free of external and infrastructure concerns.

records.name: Integration Clarity
records.definition: The degree to which relationships between contexts are made explicit and understandable.

records.name: Object Count
records.definition: The degree to which modeling many concepts as distinct value objects increases the number of objects.

records.name: Persistence Simplicity
records.definition: The degree to which a rich domain model complicates straightforward mapping to storage.

records.name: Simple CRUD
records.definition: The degree to which a full domain model adds overhead where simple create-read-update-delete would suffice.

records.name: Map to Domain Model
records.definition: A technique for translating external or persistence data into domain types at the boundary.

records.name: Move Logic to the Domain
records.definition: A technique for moving business rules out of controllers, services and scripts into the domain objects they govern.

records.name: Extract Use Case
records.definition: A technique for moving one business operation into an application service that coordinates the domain and its ports.

records.name: Extract Domain Model
records.definition: A technique for turning procedural steps over data into domain types that hold their own rules.

records.name: Extract Query Service
records.definition: A technique for moving read-only, use-case-specific queries out of a repository into a query service.

records.name: Split Repository
records.definition: A technique for reducing a repository to persistence of one aggregate and moving everything else out of it.

records.name: Add Aggregate Invariant
records.definition: A technique for enforcing a rule across related entities inside the aggregate that owns them.

records.name: Split Bounded Context
records.definition: A technique for dividing a model that serves several meanings into contexts that each own one meaning of their terms.

records.name: Attribute-Compared Identity
records.definition: A defect in which two entities are judged to be the same by comparing their attributes instead of their identity.

records.name: Reachable Invalid State
records.definition: A defect in which a domain object can be put into a state that breaks its own rules.
